description: CRM research is more than three decades old, and hence scientific literature has accumulated over the years. Articles in this cluster attempt to consolidate fragmented CRM literature through different review techniques such as systematic reviews, narrative reviews, and meta-analysis. Studies in this cluster also explore the effectiveness of CRM in other contexts such as geographical regions, cultural contexts, and economic situations. Whereas Vrontis et al. (2020), Thomas et al. (2020), and Lafferty et al. (2016) organized CRM literature through systematic literature review, Bergkvist and Zhou (2019) and Fazli-Salehi et  al. (2019) used narrative techniques. Some of these reviews have proposed conceptual models which offer new frameworks to visualize the CRM. For instance, Lafferty et al. (2016) proposed an evolutionary process model that explains the evolution of CRM in firms and has organized CRM literature accordingly. Based on the narrative review, Bergkvist and Zhou (2019) proposed a dual path persuasion model that stipulates the direct transfer of affect from cause to the brand and indirectly through attributed motive. Fazli-Salehi et al. (2019) gives a comprehensive model of CRM with customer, company, and cause as the critical components. Through meta-analysis, Rego et al. (2021) and Fan et al. (2022) investigated the factors affecting the effectiveness of CRM and its impact, respectively. It is interesting to note that bibliometric review by Singh and Dhir (2019), though recent, does not appear in this cluster. The possible reason could be the wide scope of the study as it deals with both CRM and social marketing, and hence may not be sharing adequate common references with the other articles in this cluster. Similarly, Bhatti et al. (2022) does not appear in this cluster as it is not part of the sample, since we had drawn our sample before its publication. As CRM literature is approaching the mature stage, it is being researched in different geographical regions, and cross-country analysis is gaining traction, as evidenced by the articles in this cluster. The study by Ferraris et al. (2019) examines the impact of CRM on purchase intention among Italian (individualist) and Brazilian (collectivist) consumers. Santoro et al. (2020) investigated CRM’s impact on brand loyalty among Italian and Japanese consumers. Cosgrave and O’Dwyer (2020) investigated the perception of CRM among millennials belonging to 17 different countries pursuing education in Ireland (developed market) and UAE (developing market). An exploratory study by Priporas et  al. (2019) conducted in Greece investigated consumers’ response to CRM during the economic crisis. Thus, this set of articles forms a sub-cluster within the central cluster and is focused on examining CRM in countries at different levels of development, cultural orientations, and economic stability. To sum up, this cluster is mainly focused on consolidating the CRM literature using different techniques and proposing conceptual models to visualize CRM from different perspectives. Further, the studies focus on investigating CRM in other contexts. Novice and established researchers in CRM could benefit immensely by going through the review articles in this cluster, as most literature reviews give an overview of the field for three decades and future research directions. The empirical papers in this cluster are more focused on investigating the contextual effect of nationality, culture, and gender are helpful in fine-grained analysis and understanding of CRM.

Articles in this cluster predominantly focus on congruence among the company, cause, and consumer on consumer CRM responses. These articles also investigate the interaction of congruencies with the product type and donation size. Congruence refers to the degree of fit between different entities. The degree of fit determines the outcome of the CRM. The company-cause fit has been intensively researched over the years and still attracts the significant attention of CRM researchers. The studies have generated mixed results. Some have concluded that low congruency elicits favorable consumer responses (Barone et al., 2000; Koschate-Fischer et al., 2012; Robinson et al., 2012). Others found high congruency to be more effective in eliciting favorable responses (Baghi & Antonetti, 2017; Roy, 2010). Since the literature on the fit between company and cause has generated ambivalent results over the years, studies in this cluster have attempted to define what constitutes fit and then analyze various relations among variables of CRM by different authors. Mendini et al. (2018) conceptualized and classified fit as taxonomic fit (based on similar features) and thematic fit (based on relations between the company and cause in the shared context). And empirically concluded that taxonomic fit between brand and cause enhances skepticism and reduces consumers’ response to CRM, whereas thematic fit reduces doubt and improves willingness to purchase. Chang and Liu (2012) classified fit into complementary fit and consistent fit and examined their relationship with the product type. Consistent fit refers to a cause consistent with brand image. It can easily activate nodes in the associative memory network of the consumers, thus affecting the easy recall and positive affect transfer. There will be no elaboration. In contrast, complementary fit refers to causes not related to the company’s brand image. Complementary fit triggers heightened information processing and greater elaboration. The hedonic product generates better results with complementary fit and utilitarian with the consistent fit (Chang & Liu, 2012). Further, a higher donation level enhances the beneficial effect of complementary fit (Chang & Liu, 2012; Zdravkovic et al., 2010) identified the dimensions of fit between brand and social cause as market structure fit and prominence fit. Causes vary in scope, type, and acuteness and differentially affect consumer responses in CRM (Vanhamme et  al., 2012). Similarly, consumers differ in their familiarity with causes and the importance of the cause, cause involvement, and identification. Whereas the study by Vyravene and Rabbanee (2016) investigates cause familiarity and cause importance on consumer moral judgment of CRM campaigns, the study by Vanhamme et al. (2012) reports the cause identification as the mechanism that mediates the CRM cause effect on positive consumer response. In summary, articles in this cluster investigate the congruence between companies and causes and between consumers and causes.

Donation is the quintessential feature of CRM. Donations vary in magnitude, form (monetary vs. non-monetary), framing (abstract vs. concrete), and transparency. Thus, they differentially impact consumer response. Articles in this cluster focus on issues and concerns related to donations, such as how much to donate (KoschateFischer et al., 2016; Müller et al., 2014), in what form to donate (Müller et al., 2014; Woodroof et al., 2019), how to frame and communicate donation related information (Müller et al., 2014; Singh & Duque, 2020). These articles also research the relation of donations with firm and cause fit (Koschate-Fischer et al., 2016), CRM skepticism (Fennell et al., 2020), and perceived fairness in the event of price increase (Fennell et al., 2020; Koschate-Fischer et al., 2016). Further, few notable studies investigate the impact of CRM on firm and shareholder value (Das et al., 2020; Woodroof et al., 2019) and actual sales through field experiments (Andrews et al., 2014). The study by Müller et al. (2014) explores the tradeoff perceived between availing discount (thus, benefiting self) versus donation (thus, helping others); and its relationship with donation/discount size. They reported that higher donation size reduced brand choice and brand image. However, in the absence of a tradeoff (where consumers need not incur any loss of discount), higher donations lead to higher brand choices (Müller et al., 2014). The study by Andrews et al. (2014) investigated the combined effect of discount and donation on sales and found that consumer response was most favorable for a moderate price discount level and unfavorable for very low and very high price discounts. If the discount level was too high, it led to losing the warm glow associated with donations, thus leading to a less favorable response. Going beyond the tradeoff between discount/donation, Koschate-Fischer et  al. (2016) investigated the impact of price rise and consumer response (perceived fairness), as some firms increase prices in commensuration with CRM. They reported that consumer perceived fairness would be high if a high fit between cause and company, high firm CSR reputation, and announcing CRM and price rise are simultaneous (rather than staggered). Lack of transparency in CRM donations and, consequently, absence of trust in CRM is a significant concern in CRM campaigns. Singh and Duque (2020) investigated this theme with two donation formats. One, with compressed format (total price of $79 with the amount being donated to charity $5), another with separated form (Price of $74 with the amount being donated to charity $5), and reported that 505 T. Moreover, the high transparency helps meet the expectations of other stakeholders, such as ‘Better Business Bureau’s Standards for Charity Accountability’, which advocates transparency in donation communication. The above studies predominantly study consumer response to CRM in lab conditions. However, few studies in this cluster have examined the efficacy of CRM in natural situations through event studies. For instance, through event studies, Das et al. (2020) and Woodroof et al. (2019) attempted to evaluate the effect of CRM announcements on shareholders’ value. However, in their findings, they are contradictory to each other. Whereas a study by Das et al. (2020) concludes that CRM leads to the appreciation of shareholders’ value, Woodroof et  al. (2019) conclude the opposite. Therefore, there is much scope for further investigation of this exciting area.

The central feature of CRM is for-profit firms claiming to support nonprofit organizations engaged in causes. Consumers sense some incoherence in such claims and find it hard to reconcile conflicting objectives of for-profit firms pursuing nonprofit goals. In the process, attribute motive to the firms’ CRM actions. This tendency to attribute motive to a firm differs across different categories of consumers based on their level of skepticism. Articles in this cluster primarily focus on consumer skepticism, its antecedents and negative consequences (Amawate & Deb, 2021; Deb et al., 2021; Shazly & Mahrous, 2020), and ways to minimize or avoid adverse effects through appropriate communication strategies (Bae, 2018, 2020a, b). In the marketing context, consumer skepticism refers to an individual’s tendency to disbelieve, mistrust, or question the firms’ communication claims. Amawate & Deb (2021) and Deb et  al. (2021) identified factors such as the firm’s image, the image of NPO, CRM communication, perceived firm’s motive, and the cultural conditioning of the consumers as antecedents of CRM Skepticism. The positive image of firms and NPOs, good CRM message, positive perceived firms’ motives, and collectivist mindset reduce consumer skepticism and elicit favorable CRM responses (Amawate & Deb, 2021; Deb et al., 2021). Consumer skepticism is a significant challenge to the success of CRM. Studies by Mikyeung Bae majorly focus on overcoming CRM skepticism through a communication strategy. When confronted with the CRM message, highly skeptical consumers tend to disengage from the message. However, this phenomenon varies based on the message framing, such as ad type (information or emotional) and valence of the message (positive or negative emotion). Through empirical research, Bae (2020b) showed that highly skeptical consumers could be engaged and persuaded through negative emotional advertisements such as sad appeal. Further, consumers who are dispositional skeptics can be persuaded with a two-sided message (wherein firm disclose the benefit accruing to self as well as the public through CRM) rather than a single-sided message (wherein firm specify benefit accruing to the public through CRM) (Bae, 2018). In summary, this cluster focus on one of the least researched area of CRM with significant implications for CRM success. Consumer skepticism is a significant hurdle that needs to be overcome. By identifying the antecedents of skepticism, their impact on consumer CRM responses, and investigating communication strategies to manage highly skeptical consumers, articles in this cluster contribute to the advancement of consumer behavior and communication literature.
